market_definition.boundary_notes: The boundary is the whole question here. Independent estimates treat 'financial close and reconciliation software' as a category of $6-8B, while figures above $80B are rollups of the entire office-of-the-CFO software stack including ERP [S1]. Reconciliation proper is the matching of bank statements and other external records against the ledger; it is a step inside the close, and in many mid-market shops it is a module of the ERP rather than a separate purchase [S2]. Any sizing that does not say which of those three boundaries it used is not usable.
how_analysts_segment_it: By boundary: reconciliation only, versus the whole financial close, versus the full office-of-the-CFO stack including ERP [S1]
By customer size: mid-market is called out as a distinct slice with its own estimate [S1]
By delivery: standalone reconciliation vendor versus a native module bundled with the ERP the finance team already runs [S2]

tam_estimates.methodology: Independent composite of 2026 estimates for the financial close and reconciliation software category, explicitly excluding the ERP rollup

tam_estimates.source: Reconciliation software sizing, independent composite — mid-market slice
tam_estimates.methodology: Same composite, narrowed to the mid-market reconciliation slice specifically

tam_estimates.source: Figures circulating in vendor marketing, as characterised by the independent composite rather than observed directly
tam_estimates.methodology: Rollup of the entire office-of-the-CFO software stack including ERP. Reported here because it is the number a founder is most likely to encounter, not because it is credible for this category.

sizing.consensus_view: For the category as normally defined, $6-8B in 2026, with the mid-market reconciliation slice at $900M-1.3B [S1]. Only one independent source was available, so 'consensus' overstates it — this is one composite, not a convergence of several.
sizing.why_estimates_diverge: Divergence here is not measurement noise, it is boundary choice. The $80B+ figures include the entire office-of-the-CFO stack including ERP; the $6-8B figures cover close and reconciliation software as its own category [S1]. The two are not competing estimates of the same object. Confidence is set low because only one source addressed sizing at all — the range it gives is internally consistent, but nothing independent corroborates it.

tailwinds: Manual reconciliation is genuine, recurring work with an audit consequence, which makes it a budgeted pain rather than a discretionary one
Incumbents moving down-market indicates they believe the mid-market segment is buying [S2]
headwinds: Adoption failures cluster on source data quality — teams that cannot get clean feeds from banks and ERP see little benefit from automation, so the value depends on a precondition the vendor does not control [S3]
Native reconciliation modules ship bundled with the ERP mid-market finance teams already run, which means the buyer often already owns a good-enough option [S2]
demand_signals.buyer_budget_reality: Not established by the available research. No source gives pricing, contract values or budget behaviour for mid-market reconciliation buyers. The one structural fact on the record is that a bundled ERP module competes at no incremental line item [S2].

saturation.consolidation_activity: None seen. No source in this material reports an acquisition in this category.
saturation.why: Four named players were found, all of them established rather than emerging, and two of them arriving in the mid-market from above within the last two years [S2]. That is the profile of a category being consolidated downward rather than one being opened up. No source here reports new entrants, pricing movement or acquisitions, so three of the five saturation signals are genuinely unknown rather than benign — 'a defensible niche remains' rests on the $900M-1.3B mid-market slice being real [S1] and on the observation that incumbent attention arrived recently enough that positions are probably not yet fixed. It is a weak read and should be treated as one.

what_would_prevent_it: Workflow depth beyond what a bundled module attempts — genuinely hard reconciliation cases the ERP's native feature does not handle
Feed engineering as the real product: if the durable value is getting and keeping clean bank and ERP data, that is operational work an ERP vendor has less incentive to do well for every bank [S3]
Audit defensibility, if auditors come to expect evidence a native module does not produce
A buyer who runs several ERPs and therefore cannot consolidate on any one vendor's native module
absorption_risk.notes: The verdict is 'feature' rather than 'contested' for one specific reason, and it is not a general suspicion about bundling: two of the four named competitors already ship this function inside the ERP the target customer already runs [S2]. That is not a forecast of absorption, it is absorption that has already occurred in part of the segment. What keeps it from being settled is that bundled modules are frequently shallow, and the evidence here says nothing about how capable those native modules actually are. No precedents are cited because none of the mechanisms in this material match a documented case closely enough — asserting antivirus or file sync as a parallel would be my own analogy rather than anything the research supports.

open_source_landscape.evidence_for_the_gap: No source in this material names an open-source reconciliation project, reports adoption for one, or discusses open source in this category at all. `applicable` is set false on that basis. This is an absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence: it means the research did not cover the question, not that the category has been shown to have no open-source dimension. The capability_gap and gap_trend values are placeholders required by the schema and carry no finding — they should not be read as an assessment.
open_source_landscape.notes: Treat this section as unresearched. The absorption threat established by the evidence is bundling by ERP vendors [S2], not open-source commoditization, and inventing projects to fill this section would misrepresent where the risk actually sits.

adjacent_markets.size_note: Not sized here. The independent composite notes that ERP is what inflates the $80B+ figures, which is the only quantitative statement available about the relationship [S1].
adjacent_markets.why_it_matters: The ERP is the system of record on one side of every reconciliation and, for NetSuite and Sage customers, already ships the function [S2]. This company competes with the ERP whether or not it intends to.

adjacent_markets.market: Financial close management (the wider close, beyond reconciliation)
adjacent_markets.size_note: Included in the $6-8B category figure, which covers financial close and reconciliation together [S1]
adjacent_markets.why_it_matters: The established vendors sell into the whole close, so a reconciliation-only product meets them as part of a larger purchase rather than head-on [S2].

Adoption fails on feed quality rather than on the reconciliation tool [S3], so this upstream layer determines whether the product delivers value at all. It is the most plausible place for a defensible position and the most plausible place to get stuck.

research_gaps: Sizing rests on a single composite [S1]. Nothing corroborates it, which is why sizing_confidence is low despite the range being internally coherent.
No pricing, contract value, gross margin or CAC payback data for this category was available, so the economics section is unfilled rather than estimated.
No funding rounds, valuations or acquisitions were reported, so both the funding environment and the consolidation half of the saturation read are unknown.

New-entrant flow is unknown, which is the single most important missing saturation signal — four established players with no visibility into whether anyone new is arriving cannot distinguish a maturing category from a closing one.
Nothing addresses open source in this category, so that section is unresearched rather than assessed.

The capability of the bundled NetSuite and Sage reconciliation modules is not described [S2]. Whether they are shallow or substantial decides how much room a specialist has, and it is the highest-value gap to close.
Nothing in the material speaks to this company's own traction claims [C5, C6, C7] or its valuation [C10]; those are diligence questions, not market-research ones.
